Known-good QA fixture

Activity practice · about 14 min
Objectives
  • Complete a safe interaction and explain why it is safe.
  1. Activity 1
  2. Activity 2
  3. Activity 3

Teaching

Direct controls work without network access. Complete work stays in place when you revisit an activity.

Another way to think about itOptional example

A shopper walks one aisle and places only useful items into a fresh basket.

The same select-and-gather idea can build a new collection from existing items.

Where this fits

Decision: Decide whether an effect should stay on this page or cross a boundary.

Good fit: Use the local control for a bounded, self-contained practice change.

Choose something else when: The work must contact another system or coordinate several dependent steps.

Activity 1 — Your task: choose a safe action

Choose the safe action below your note, then compare it with the explained result.

Need a hint?Hint 1 of 2 for Activity 1

Where to act: Classify each result control below your note.

Next step: Decide whether each effect remains in this page or crosses a boundary.

Another hintAnother hint, 2 of 2 for Activity 1

Where to act: Inspect the on-page feedback region after trying a control.

Next step: Use where its result appears as evidence for your boundary classification.

What success looks like

Your note remains when you leave and return, and the local result is explained.

0 of 1

Challenge (optional)

Optional time: about 2 minutes

Success criteria: Write two safe actions using only the controls already taught.

Activity 2 — Your task: explain your choice

Explain in the field below why your first action stays local.

Activity checks

Your explanation names the boundary that keeps the action safe.

Back to activity 1

Activity 3 — Your task: recap

Review your saved note and explanation, then state the boundary.

What success looks like

You can state which action is safe and why.

Back to activity 2

Recap

Use direct controls and check resulting state.

Printed alternative: choose a local control, then explain the observed in-page result.
